sources.title: Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar (Q964111), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-05): English label 'Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar', description 'Philosopher, academic, writer, translator, entrepreneur, social reformer and philanthropist (1820-1891)', birth 26 September 1820, death 29 July 1891, image Ishwarchandra Vidyasagar.jpg; no Korean label. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Banglapedia (Asiatic Society of Bangladesh), 'Vidyasagar, Ishwar Chandra' (full entry read). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Sanskrit scholar, writer, educationist and philanthropist; studied at Sanskrit College 1829-1841 and earned the title Vidyasagar by 1839; resigned the Assistant Secretary post in July 1847 after obstacles from the conservative secretary; returned in December 1850 and became Principal in January 1851, opened the college to all Hindus, introduced nominal fees, moved the weekly holiday to Sunday, made English compulsory and taught grammar and mathematics through Bangla and English as well as Sanskrit; as assistant inspector from 1855 opened Bangla schools in four districts (twenty in a couple of years), a normal school, and a village school almost entirely with his own money; opened thirty-four more girls' schools in 1857-58 until differences with the director of public instruction led him to resign; took over the Metropolitan Institution in 1864; his textbooks (Barnaparichay and others) ran dozens of editions, and he is credited with creating a literary Bangla prose, though 'some contemporary writers' called him little more than a translator, which the entry rejects. Also records his widow-remarriage writing and petitions (context only here; unscored). Reference work; its praise is retrospective and the entry differs from other sources on some dates (it gives the Widow Remarriage Act as 1857 where other sources say 1856), so no row depends on a date.

EBSCO Research Starters, 'Iswar Chandra Vidyasagar' by Rane C. Chakravorty (2024; the whole entry read). An independent modern encyclopedia: studied about twelve and a half years at Sanskrit College, won prizes at every stage and was given the title Vidyasagar after a Hindu-law examination in 1839; as head of the Bengali department at Fort William College he studied English and Hindi privately; started his own press and book depository to print his books; as principal for eight years admitted all castes, made English compulsory and wrote new Sanskrit grammar textbooks; managed the Calcutta Training School from 1864; was honorary secretary of the Bethune School and as school inspector opened women's schools; 'refined the Bengali alphabet' in Baranaparichay; Tagore 'credited Vidyasagar with effectively establishing the beauty of Bengali prose'; notes that his campaigns against polygamy and for a higher age of consent were not achieved in his lifetime. Also calls him an atheist and an 'embodiment of compassion' (not used).

Amiya P. Sen (historian), 'Remembering Iswarchandra Vidyasagar', Sahapedia (read in full). An independent historian's essay that combines praise with criticism: Tagore's 'Vidyasagar-charit' is described as the best commentary and portrays a man of effort, self-respect and self-determination unlike his contemporaries; Vidyasagar 'opposed state spending on traditional Hindu education' and urged Western learning, favoured Baconian thought; he was criticised by contemporaries such as Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay for relying on scriptural sanctions for social legislation, and his later reputation has been contested (statue vandalism in 1970 and 2019). COUNTER-VOICE for the sources above. Short magazine-style essay; its characterisations are interpretive.

Subal Chandra Mitra, 'Isvar Chandra Vidyasagar: A Story of His Life and Work' (Calcutta: New Bengal Press, 1902), with an introduction by R. C. Dutt, Internet Archive scan read in the parts on his Fort William College years, the Sanskrit College principalship (the 20 March 1851 report on admitting Kayastha boys, the professors' objections, his threat to resign), his resignation correspondence of 1857-58 (his own letters to the Director of Public Instruction and Lieutenant-Governor are reproduced) and the relief of the poor during a famine and scarcity in his home district (a Commissioner's letter of Government acknowledgment is reproduced). Early English biography by an admirer who says he does not gloss over shortcomings and draws on Behari Lal Sarkar's Bengali life; Dutt's introduction is a personal acquaintance's tribute; the book quotes C. E. Buckland, 'Bengal under the Lieutenant-Governors', on the 1858 conflict (read only as quoted). Admiring and anecdotal in places (anecdotes introduced by 'it is said' are not scored); the reproduced letters and reports are the strongest part.

Sivanath Sastri, 'Ramtanu Lahiri, Brahman and Reformer: A History of the Renaissance in Bengal' (London: Swan Sonnenschein, 1907; translated from the Bengali; Internet Archive scan from the University of California Libraries, item ramtanulahiribra00sastiala, possible-copyright-status NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT). Portrait source only: the book contains a full-page engraved plate captioned 'PANDIT ISWARA CHANDRA VIDYASAGARA.' facing page 57; its text about Vidyasagar (a teacher at Fort William College who wrote Vetala-panchabinsati in 1847) is not used for any row.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_vidyasagar_banglapedia, src_vidyasagar_ebsco, src_vidyasagar_mitra1902 | 1850-1858 | encyclopedias, early biography with reproduced documents] As principal of Sanskrit College he opened it to all Hindus, introduced fees, moved the holiday to Sundays, made English compulsory and taught grammar and mathematics through Bangla and English (Banglapedia, EBSCO); Mitra reproduces his 20 March 1851 report asking that Kayastha boys be admitted, records the professors' objections, his scriptural counter-arguments and his stated readiness to resign if it failed, and the authorities approving it. He also opened Bangla and girls' schools across four districts from 1855 (Banglapedia). Two independent modern reference works and reproduced documents agree on the actions; the 'hue and cry' framing is Mitra's. RUBRIC_CORRECTION (lead review, before eligibility): proactive_agency lowered from 78 / 0.6 to 74 / 0.56 because Banglapedia, EBSCO and an admiring 1902 biography prefaced by a friend all tell one standard story.

autonomy_need.rationale: [src_vidyasagar_banglapedia, src_vidyasagar_ebsco, src_vidyasagar_mitra1902 | 1847-1858 | encyclopedias, early biography with reproduced letters] He resigned the Assistant Secretary post in 1847 when his syllabus plans met the conservative secretary's resistance (Banglapedia, EBSCO), and resigned all his government posts in 1858 after differences with the Director of Public Instruction, the later resignation documented by his own letters, which say he cannot consistently alter his letter of resignation, and by Buckland's statement that he 'came into conflict' with the Director (Mitra); Mitra adds that he refused to soften an examination for a superior at Fort William College (single-source). The pattern of leaving posts rather than yielding is documented; the motives and the remark about self-respect come from Mitra's admiring account. RUBRIC_CORRECTION (lead review, before eligibility): autonomy_need lowered from 74 / 0.55 to 70 / 0.5 because the resignation episodes come from the admiring 1902 biography.

mastery_orientation.rationale: [src_vidyasagar_banglapedia, src_vidyasagar_ebsco, src_vidyasagar_mitra1902 | 1829-1845 | encyclopedias, early biography] Banglapedia and EBSCO describe twelve years at Sanskrit College across grammar, literature, rhetoric, Vedanta, jurisprudence, logic and Hindu law, with prizes at every stage and the title Vidyasagar by 1839, and EBSCO and Dutt's introduction (in Mitra) say he took up English and Hindi while working as head pandit at Fort William College. Two independent modern references agree on the study; the early life stories (poverty, study by streetlight) are told by admirers and are not scored. RUBRIC_CORRECTION (lead review, before eligibility): mastery_orientation lowered from 74 / 0.52 to 70 / 0.48 because early-study evidence is the same admiring biography and encyclopedias.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_vidyasagar_banglapedia, src_vidyasagar_ebsco, src_vidyasagar_mitra1902 | 1847-1860 | encyclopedias, early biography] Banglapedia credits him with creating a literary Bangla prose through Vetal Panchavimshati (1847), Shakuntala and Sitar Banabas, adapting rather than merely translating, and EBSCO reports Tagore crediting him with establishing the beauty of Bengali prose; Dutt's 1902 introduction says elegant modern Bengali prose was created under his formative touch. Banglapedia itself notes that some contemporary writers called him little more than a translator and textbook writer, and the praise is retrospective literary judgement rather than documented behaviour, so the row is moderate and low-confidence. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): top-risk row; lowered from 70 / 0.52 to 64 / 0.46 because the claim rests on later praise and Banglapedia records contemporaries who disputed his originality.

resourcefulness.rationale: [src_vidyasagar_ebsco, src_vidyasagar_mitra1902, src_vidyasagar_banglapedia | 1847-1864 | encyclopedias, early biography] He set up his own press and book depository to print and sell his books (EBSCO); Mitra says the Sanskrit Press began with a borrowed Rs 600 shared equally with Madan Mohan Tarkalankar before he became sole proprietor; his textbooks 'ran dozens of editions' and were prescribed in every school in Bengal (Banglapedia), which supplied the income he lived on after leaving government service (Mitra, quoting him). Documented in outline by two sources but the commercial details are Mitra's, so moderate.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_vidyasagar_banglapedia, src_vidyasagar_ebsco | 1841-1864 | encyclopedias] His activity spanned Sanskrit grammar, Bengali primers and readers, literary adaptation from Sanskrit and English (including a Bengali version of The Comedy of Errors), publishing, school inspection and college management, and his readers drew on European biography and science. These are adjacent educational and literary fields rather than unrelated ones, so the row is moderate.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_vidyasagar_banglapedia, src_vidyasagar_mitra1902, src_vidyasagar_ebsco | 1855-1860s | encyclopedias, early biography with reproduced letter] Banglapedia says he founded a school in his own village almost entirely with his own money and persuaded local people to establish a girls' school at Bardhaman (1857), and EBSCO says he opened women's schools at his own expense until reimbursed; Mitra reproduces a Commissioner's letter conveying the Government's acknowledgment of his relief of the poor during the recent scarcity in Hooghly district. Education and relief work are documented by two sources, but admiring ones for the relief details; no political activism is scored. RUBRIC_CORRECTION (lead review, before eligibility): impact_motivation lowered from 74 / 0.52 to 70 / 0.48 because motive is read from an admiring biography and reference entries.

portrait.source: Engraved portrait captioned 'PANDIT ISWARA CHANDRA VIDYASAGARA.', plate in Sivanath Sastri, 'Ramtanu Lahiri, Brahman and Reformer: A History of the Renaissance in Bengal' (London: Swan Sonnenschein, 1907), from the University of California Libraries copy digitised by the Internet Archive. The engraver and the photograph or drawing it was made from are not named in the book, so it is treated as a later engraved depiction made about sixteen years after his death, though it matches the same likeness printed in 1906 and 1911 publications. The file is a crop of the plate and its caption from the full-page scan (1360 x 2010), downscaled to 812 x 1200 with no upscaling.

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: PLAUSIBLE (alt-dependent) (lead) / REPLACEMENT USED (same man, better-lettered plate). Lead (Andhra Patrika 1911 Ugadi issue, Internet Archive item andhrapatrikasamvatsaradisanchika1911; Commons file Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagarudu1911.jpg 940 x 1264, tagged PD-India, issue dated 12 April 1911): HOLDER RECORD CHECKED: the archive's metadata gives title, creator 'Andhra Patrika', date 1911 and language Telugu, with NO possible-copyright-status field and no further rights wording; the plate on Commons carries no caption (the OCR line near the page reads in Telugu 'this is Vidyasagarudu', so identity there is textual, not a printed caption on the image); a blurry halftone of a Telugu weekly. It is usable as a corroborating image but not the best route. Also rejected: Commons 'Ishwarchandra Vidyasagar.jpg' (Wikidata P18; source vivekananda.net, author unknown, generic PD-old), 'Vidyasagar, at the end of his life.jpg' and 'Vidyasagar young.jpg' (unknown author, generic PD-India), and the 2021 photograph and statue images (modern rights). REPLACEMENT USED: engraved plate 'PANDIT ISWARA CHANDRA VIDYASAGARA.' in Sivanath Sastri, 'Ramtanu Lahiri, Brahman and Reformer' (London: Swan Sonnenschein, 1907), Internet Archive item ramtanulahiribra00sastiala from the University of California Libraries (metadata date 1907, publisher London: Swan Sonnenschein, possible-copyright-status NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT); a book published in London in 1907 is public domain in the United States (published before 1931). The plate sits on leaf 101 (facing p. 57) of 316; the leaf was downloaded at full size (1940 x 3214) and the plate and its caption were cropped (1360 x 2010) and downscaled to 812 x 1200 (no upscaling). IMAGE CHECK (looked at the file): a half-length engraving of a man in a draped shawl, short curled hair, captioned 'PANDIT ISWARA CHANDRA VIDYASAGARA.', which matches the claimed sitter; the same likeness appears in the 1911 Andhra Patrika halftone and the 1906 'Bengal Celebrities' plate, so the three reproductions agree on the sitter. The engraver and the photograph or source drawing are not named in the book, so kind is historical_depiction (it is likely engraved from a lifetime photograph, but that is undocumented). PREFLIGHT (identity/QID/region): Wikidata Q964111 verified live (label 'Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar', 1820-1891); no production or candidate collision (prod65.txt, candidate directory). Korean name: no Korean Wikipedia or Wikidata label, so '이슈와르 찬드라 비디야사가르' is a recorded standard transliteration. Region south_asia (Bengal), nationality IN, polity British Raj, era 19th_century. ZERO POLITICS / ACTIVISM LIMIT: scored as educator, scholar, textbook author and Bengali prose writer only; his widow-remarriage writing and petitions, the campaign against polygamy and the age-of-consent debates are social-reform context, appear only as a clause in one achievement card (no row, no moment), and his religious views (EBSCO calls him an atheist; Sahapedia says he had little interest in religion) are not scored. ATTRIBUTION: attributable (lead) / CONFIRMED: reproduced letters and reports, two independent encyclopedias and a historian agree on the actions. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Banglapedia entry (src_vidyasagar_banglapedia). SOURCES READ: Banglapedia (full), EBSCO Research Starters (full), Sahapedia essay by Amiya P. Sen (full), Mitra 1902 biography with Dutt's introduction (the chapters on Fort William, the Sanskrit College, the 1857-58 resignation and the famine relief), Sastri 1907 plate page. PERSPECTIVES: a Bangladeshi national encyclopedia, a modern reference encyclopedia, a modern historian, and an admiring 1902 Bengali biographer with an introduction by R. C. Dutt and a quoted British official (Buckland). COUNTER-VOICE: Sahapedia (Bankim's criticism of his scriptural method, his later contested reputation), Banglapedia's note that contemporaries called him mainly a translator, the professors' objections in Mitra and the satire and petitions of orthodox opponents in Dutt's introduction (context). Non-self behavioural sources: Banglapedia, EBSCO, Mitra's reproduced documents. NOT OPENED: Hatcher's 'Idioms of Improvement' and 'Vidyasagar: The Life and After-life' (paywalled or lending), Curley's and Conlon's reviews, Asok Sen's critical study 'Iswar Chandra Vidyasagar and His Elusive Milestones' (lending-only), Tagore's essay in Bengali, Behari Lal Sarkar's Bengali biography, Buckland's book itself. Date discrepancies (Barnaparichay 1851 vs 1855; Widow Remarriage Act 1856 vs 1857) mean no row depends on those dates. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): top-risk rows reviewed: creative_originality (70/0.52 lowered to 64/0.46: retrospective praise and a documented contemporary dissent), proactive_agency (kept: 78/0.60 is supported by two independent encyclopedias and reproduced documents), autonomy_need (kept: both resignations are documented by letters or two sources). MAJOR ACHIEVEMENT SELF-GATE: first-pass PASS on primary, top omission (widow-remarriage writing placed in a card clause as context), identity, significance-over-novelty and side-project (his press and the Metropolitan Institution are in service of the educational contribution, not a displacing side venture); nothing corrected.
